{{Short description|Algebras arising in harmonic analysis}}
{{citation style|date=February 2012}}
'''Fourier''' and related [[Associative algebra|algebras]] occur naturally in the [[harmonic analysis]] of [[locally compact]] [[Group (mathematics)|groups]]. They play an important role in the [[duality theory|duality theories]] of these groups. The Fourier–Stieltjes algebra and the Fourier–Stieltjes transform on the Fourier algebra of a locally compact group were introduced by [[Pierre Eymard]] in 1964.

==Definition==

===Informal===
Let <math>G</math> be a locally compact abelian group, and <math>\hat{G}</math> the [[Pontryagin dual|dual group]] of <math>G</math>. Then <math> L_1(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math> is the space of all functions on <math>\hat{G}</math> which are integrable with respect to the [[Haar measure]] on <math>\hat{G}</math>, and it has a [[Banach algebra]] structure where the product of two functions is [[convolution]]. We define <math>A(G) </math> to be the set of Fourier transforms of functions in <math> L_1(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math>, and it is a closed sub-algebra of <math>CB(G) </math>, the space of bounded continuous complex-valued functions on <math>G</math> with pointwise multiplication. We call <math>A(G) </math> the Fourier algebra of <math>G</math>.

Similarly, we write <math> M(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math> for the measure algebra on <math>\hat{G}</math>, meaning the convolution algebra of all finite regular [[Borel measure|Borel measures]] on <math>\hat{G}</math>.  We define <math>B(G) </math> to be the set of Fourier-Stieltjes transforms of measures in <math> M(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math>. It is a closed sub-algebra of <math>CB(G) </math>, the space of bounded continuous complex-valued functions on <math>G</math> with pointwise multiplication. We call <math>B(G) </math> the Fourier-Stieltjes algebra of <math>G</math>. Equivalently, <math>B(G) </math> can be defined as the linear span of the set <math>P(G) </math> of continuous [[Positive-definite function|positive-definite functions]] on <math>G</math>.<ref>{{eom|title=Fourier-algebra(2)|first=Jean|last=Renault}}</ref>

Since <math> L_1(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math> is naturally included in <math> M(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math>, and since the Fourier-Stieltjes transform of an <math> L_1(\hat{\mathit{G}}) </math> function is just the Fourier transform of that function, we have that <math>A(G) \subset B(G) </math>. In fact, <math>A(G) </math> is a closed ideal in <math>B(G) </math>.

===Formal===
While non-abelian groups don't have dual groups, we may still define the Fourier algebras for any locally compact group in terms of [[unitary representation|unitary representations]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Eymard | first=P. | title=L'algèbre de Fourier d'un groupe localement compact | journal=Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France | publisher=Société mathématique de France | volume=92 | issn=0037-9484 | pages=181–236 | url=https://eudml.org/doc/87049 | access-date=Mar 18, 2026}}</ref> Let <math>G</math> be a locally compact group. For any unitary representation <math>\pi</math> of <math>G</math> on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H_\pi</math>, and any <math>\xi,\eta\in H_\pi</math>, we denote by <math>\pi_{\xi,\eta}</math> the complex-valued function on <math>G</math> defined by <math>\pi_{\xi,\eta}(g)=\langle \pi(g)\xi,\eta\rangle</math>. The Fourier-Stieltjes algebra <math>B(G)</math> is then defined as the algebra of all complex functions on <math>G</math> that arise as matrix coefficients <math>\pi_{\xi,\eta}</math> for some unitary representation <math>\pi</math> of <math>G</math> and some <math>\xi,\eta\in H_\pi</math>. <math>B(G)</math> forms an algebra with pointwise addition and multiplication, as for any unitary representations <math>\pi</math> and <math>\rho</math> of <math>G</math>, <math>\pi_{\xi_1,\eta_1}+\rho_{\xi_2,\eta_2}=(\pi\oplus\rho)_{\xi_1\oplus\xi_2,\eta_1\oplus\eta_2}</math> and <math>\pi_{\xi_1,\eta_1}\rho_{\xi_2,\eta_2}=(\pi\otimes\rho)_{\xi_1\otimes\xi_2,\eta_1\otimes\eta_2}</math>. We define the norm in <math>B(G)</math> to be given by <math>\| u\|=\text{inf} \{ \| \xi\| \|\eta\| : u(g)=\langle\pi(g)\xi,\eta\rangle \text{ for some representation } \pi \}</math>. This norm makes <math>B(G)</math> a [[Banach algebra]]. We define the Fourier algebra <math>A(G)</math> to be the closed subalgebra spanned by the matrix coefficients of the left [[regular representation]] of <math>G</math> on <math>L^2(G)</math>. 

===Abelian case===
Let <math> B(\mathit{G}) </math> be a Fourier–Stieltjes algebra and <math> A(\mathit{G}) </math> be a Fourier algebra such that the locally compact group <math> \mathit{G} </math> is [[Abelian group|abelian]]. Let <math> M(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math> be the measure algebra of finite measures on <math> \widehat{G} </math> and let <math> L_1(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math> be the [[Group algebra of a locally compact group#The convolution algebra L1.28G.29|convolution algebra]] of [[Haar measure#Haar integral|integrable]] [[Function (mathematics)|function]]s on <math> \widehat{G} </math>, where <math> \widehat{\mathit{G}} </math> is the character group of the Abelian group <math> \mathit{G} </math>.

The Fourier–Stieltjes transform of a finite measure <math> \mu </math> on <math> \widehat{\mathit{G}} </math> is the function <math> \widehat{\mu} </math> on <math> \mathit{G} </math> defined by

: <math> \widehat{\mu}(x) =  \int_{\widehat{G}} \overline{X(x)} \, d \mu(X), \quad x \in G </math>

The space <math> B(\mathit{G}) </math> of these functions is an algebra under pointwise multiplication is isomorphic to the measure algebra <math> M(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math>. Restricted to <math> L_1(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math>, viewed as a subspace of <math> M(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math>, the Fourier–Stieltjes transform is the [[Fourier transform]] on <math> L_1(\widehat{\mathit{G}}) </math> and its image is, by definition, the Fourier algebra <math> A(\mathit{G}) </math>. The generalized [[Bochner theorem]] states that a [[measurable function]] on <math> \mathit{G} </math> is equal, [[almost everywhere]], to the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of a non-negative finite measure on <math> \widehat{G} </math> [[if and only if]] it is positive definite. Thus, <math> B(\mathit{G}) </math> can be defined as the [[linear span]] of the set of continuous positive-definite functions on <math> \mathit{G} </math>. This definition is still valid when <math> \mathit{G} </math> is not Abelian.

==Results==

===Helson–Kahane–Katznelson–Rudin theorem===
Let <math>A(G)</math> be the Fourier algebra of a compact group <math>G</math>. Building upon the work of [[Norbert Wiener|Wiener]], [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Lévy]], [[Israel Gelfand|Gelfand]], and [[Arne Beurling|Beurling]], in 1959 [[Henry Helson|Helson]], [[Jean-Pierre Kahane|Kahane]], [[Yitzhak Katznelson|Katznelson]], and [[Walter Rudin|Rudin]] proved that, when <math>G</math> is compact and abelian, a function f defined on a closed convex subset of the plane operates in <math>A(G)</math> if and only if <math>f</math> is real analytic.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=H. Helson |author2=J.-P. Kahane |author3=Y. Katznelson |author4=W. Rudin |s2cid=121739671 |title=The functions which operate on Fourier transforms|journal=Acta Mathematica|volume=102|issue=1–2 |year=1959|pages=135–157|url=http://www.kryakin.com/files/Acta_Mat_(2_55)/acta106_57/102/102_10.pdf|doi=10.1007/bf02559571|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1969 [[Charles F. Dunkl|Dunkl]] proved the result holds when <math>G</math> is compact and contains an infinite abelian subgroup.

===Relationship to group operator algebras===
If <math>G</math> is a locally compact group, we may define the associated [[group algebra of a locally compact group|group algebras]] <math>C^*(G)</math> to be the enveloping [[C*-algebra]] of <math>L^1(G)</math> and the [[von Neumann algebra]] <math>VN(G)</math> associated to the left regular representation <math>\lambda</math> of <math>G</math> on <math>L^2(G)</math>. Then <math>B(G)</math> is the [[Banach space]] [[dual space|dual]] of <math>C^*(G)</math> and <math>VN(G)</math> is the dual of <math>A(G)</math>. The pairing between <math>A(G)</math> and <math>VN(G)</math> is defined by, for <math>T\in VN(G)</math> and <math>u\in A(G)</math> defined <math>u(x)=\langle \lambda (x)\xi ,\eta\rangle</math>, by <math>\langle T,u\rangle=\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle</math>. 

In the case where <math>G</math> is abelian, we have <math>A(G)\cong L^1(\hat{G})</math> and <math>VN(G)\cong L^\infty(\hat{G})</math>, so this reduces to the fact that <math>L^\infty(\hat{G})</math> is the dual of
<math>L^1(\hat{G})</math>. Likewise, we have <math>C^*(G)\cong C_0(\hat{G})</math> (the algebra of continuous functions on <math>\hat{G}</math> vanishing at infinity) and <math>B(G)\cong M(\hat{G})</math>, so that <math>B(G)</math> is the dual of <math>C^*(G)</math> reduces to the fact that <math>M(\hat{G})</math> is the dual of 
<math>C_0(\hat{G})</math>.
